title: Paying suppliers: fixed price, cost plus, unit & target cost
blurb: Explain the four reimbursement methods, who carries the cost risk under each, and when each is the right choice.
question: A flood defence scheme includes a fully designed pumping station, river dredging of an unknown volume, and urgent investigation work whose scope cannot yet be defined. Which reimbursement method would suit each package, and who would carry the cost risk?

teach.h: How you pay decides who carries the risk
teach.body: A reimbursement method is the way a supplier is paid under the contract. It decides who carries the cost risk and what behaviour you encourage. The four to know: FIXED PRICE (a lump sum agreed up front), COST PLUS FEE (actual costs plus a fee), PER UNIT QUANTITY (an agreed rate for each unit delivered) and TARGET COST (an agreed target, with overruns and savings shared). Plain English: the less certain the work, the harder it is to ask a supplier to promise a price.

teach.caption: Per unit quantity is also called a schedule of rates or remeasurement. Cost plus fee is a form of cost-reimbursable contract.

head: Method
Supplier carries
Buyer carries
rows: Cost overruns on the agreed scope
Little cost risk: its fee is secure
Unit costs above the agreed rate
teach.caption: Under target cost, savings below the target are shared too, so both sides gain from efficiency.

teach.h: Why not always use fixed price?
teach.body: Fixed price looks safest for the buyer, but it only works when the scope is well defined and stable. Suppliers price a risk premium into anything uncertain, so you may pay for risks that never happen, and every change becomes a priced variation. Cost plus fee avoids that premium and lets work start before scope is clear, but the supplier has little incentive to save, so the buyer needs open-book accounting and strong cost control. Target cost sits between: a shared incentive to beat an agreed target.

root.label: How well defined is the work?

children.label: Per unit quantity
children.sub: Pay a rate per unit delivered

teach.caption: Iterative projects rarely know their total scope up front, so a single fixed price is hard to set. Common answers: a fixed price per time box (time and cost fixed, scope flexes), target cost or cost plus fee.

teach.h: Target cost and the pain/gain share
teach.body: Buyer and supplier agree a target cost. Typically the supplier is paid its actual costs as work proceeds, and at the end the difference between actual cost and target is shared using an agreed pain/gain mechanism. Come in under target and both share the saving (gain); go over and both share the overrun (pain). Because both sides win or lose together, it encourages collaboration, efficiency and openness, which is why it often appears in partnering and alliancing arrangements.

items.label: of the overrun borne by each side

teach.caption: Illustrative only: the exam does not ask you to calculate. Had the job cost £0.8m, the £200k saving would have been split instead.

teach.body: The Eastbrook scheme uses all four methods. The pumping station is fully designed, so it is let on a fixed price. River dredging is paid per cubic metre removed (per unit quantity), because nobody knows exactly how much silt there is. Urgent investigation after a breach is done on cost plus fee, as its scope cannot be defined in time. The main embankment, built by an alliance of designer and contractor, uses a target cost so both share the savings from better methods.

teach.text: Classic confusions. Under COST PLUS FEE the BUYER carries the cost risk, not the supplier, and with a percentage fee the supplier earns MORE as costs rise. Under FIXED PRICE the supplier carries cost risk, but the buyer still pays for scope changes, so the final bill can rise. PER UNIT fixes the RATE, not the total: the buyer still carries the quantity risk. TARGET COST is the one with the pain/gain share.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define the method: how the supplier is paid (lump sum, actual costs plus fee, rate per unit, or target with shared overrun and savings).
Say who carries the cost risk, and why that follows from how payment works.
Say when it is appropriate: link it to how well defined and stable the scope is.
Give a downside and how to manage it (e.g. cost plus needs strong cost control; fixed price makes changes costly).
Apply it to the scenario's package, using its facts (designed, measurable, uncertain, collaborative).
Fixed price: lump sum; supplier carries cost risk; needs a well-defined scope; changes are costly.
Cost plus fee: actual costs plus a fixed or percentage fee; buyer carries cost risk; suits uncertain scope; needs strong cost control.
Per unit quantity: agreed rate per unit; suits repeated measurable work where quantities are uncertain.
Target cost: agreed target with a pain/gain share; incentivises collaboration and efficiency.
Match the method to how certain the scope is, and place risk with whoever can best manage it.

summary: You can now explain fixed price, cost plus fee, per unit quantity and target cost, and say who carries the cost risk under each. You can also choose the right method for a package of work and justify it from how well defined its scope is.

A.q: Under a fixed price contract, which party mainly carries the risk of the supplier's costs overrunning on the agreed scope?
options: The buyer
The end users
The supplier
Both equally
A.why: The supplier has promised to deliver the agreed scope for a lump sum, so if its costs overrun, it bears the loss.

whyNot.0: The buyer pays the agreed lump sum; it only pays more if it changes the scope.
whyNot.1: End users are not party to the payment terms.
whyNot.3: Sharing overruns describes a target cost pain/gain mechanism, not fixed price.

A.q: Which description matches a cost plus fee contract?
options: Actual costs paid, plus a fixed or percentage fee
One lump sum agreed before the work begins
An agreed rate paid for each unit delivered
A target agreed, with overruns and savings shared
A.why: Under cost plus fee, the buyer reimburses the supplier's actual costs and adds an agreed fee, either fixed or a percentage.

whyNot.1: A lump sum agreed up front is fixed price.
whyNot.2: Paying a rate for each unit delivered is per unit quantity.
whyNot.3: A target with shared overruns and savings is target cost.

A.q: A contractor resurfaces footpaths and is paid an agreed rate for every square metre completed. Which reimbursement method is this?
options: Fixed lump sum
Cost plus fee
Target cost
Per unit quantity
A.why: Paying an agreed rate for each measured unit (here, square metres) is per unit quantity, also called a schedule of rates.

whyNot.0: A lump sum would be one price for the whole job, regardless of area.
whyNot.1: Cost plus fee reimburses actual costs, not a rate per unit.
whyNot.2: Target cost compares actual cost with an agreed target and shares the difference.

B.q: A team must investigate a contaminated site, and nobody will know the extent of the work until it begins. Which reimbursement method is MOST appropriate, and why?
options: Fixed price, as the buyer wants certainty
Cost plus fee, as the scope is too uncertain
Per unit, as the units are clearly defined
Target cost, as a target is easy to set here
B.why: When scope cannot be defined, cost plus fee lets work start and pays actual costs. The buyer carries the cost risk, so it must control costs closely.

whyNot.0: A supplier asked for a fixed price on unknown work would add a large risk premium, or refuse to bid.
whyNot.2: There are no clearly defined, measurable units of work here.
whyNot.3: A realistic target cannot be set when nobody knows the extent of the work.

B.q: Which statement about a target cost contract is correct?
options: The supplier keeps all savings below target
The buyer pays the target whatever happens
It suits only small, one-off purchases
Overruns and savings are shared by formula
B.why: A target cost contract shares overruns (pain) and savings (gain) between buyer and supplier using an agreed mechanism.

whyNot.0: Savings are shared, not kept wholly by the supplier.
whyNot.1: Paying a set sum whatever happens describes fixed price.
whyNot.2: Target cost is typically used on larger, collaborative work, not small one-off purchases.

B.q: A buyer chose a fixed price for a well-defined building package. Midway, the client asks for an extra floor. What is the MOST likely consequence?
options: The buyer pays for it as a priced change
The supplier must absorb the extra cost
The contract becomes cost plus automatically
The extra floor is split under pain/gain
B.why: Fixed price covers the agreed scope only. A change in scope is priced as a variation, which the buyer pays for, often at a premium.

whyNot.1: The supplier carries overruns on the AGREED scope, not the cost of new scope the buyer adds.
whyNot.2: The reimbursement method does not change automatically; the change is handled through change control.
whyNot.3: Pain/gain sharing belongs to target cost contracts.

C.q:
Which TWO statements about cost risk are correct?
1) Under cost plus fee, the buyer carries the cost risk
2) Under fixed price, the buyer carries the cost risk
3) Under per unit quantity, the buyer carries the quantity risk
4) Under target cost, the supplier carries all the risk
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Under cost plus fee the buyer pays actual costs, so it carries cost risk. Under per unit quantity the rate is fixed but the buyer pays for however many units are needed.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: under fixed price the supplier carries the cost risk on the agreed scope.
whyNot.1: Both are wrong: fixed price puts cost risk on the supplier, and target cost shares it.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: target cost shares overruns and savings between both parties.

C.q: A buyer has placed a cost plus percentage fee contract and notices that the supplier seems relaxed about rising costs. What is the MOST likely reason, and the best response?
options: It is a fixed price; ignore the rising costs
Higher costs raise its fee; tighten control
The supplier carries the risk; let it pay
Overruns are shared; wait for the final split
C.why: With a percentage fee, the supplier's fee grows as costs grow, so it has little incentive to save. The buyer carries the cost risk and must apply strong cost control, such as open-book checks and approvals.

whyNot.0: It is a cost plus contract, not fixed price, and the buyer is the one exposed.
whyNot.2: Under cost plus fee the BUYER carries the cost risk.
whyNot.3: Shared overruns belong to target cost, not cost plus fee.

C.q: A software team will deliver a product iteratively in fixed two-week time boxes, with scope prioritised by the product owner. Which payment approach fits BEST?
options: One fixed price for the whole final product
Per unit, paying for each line of code
Cost plus fee with no cost controls at all
A fixed price per time box, scope flexing
C.why: In iterative work time and cost are fixed per time box while scope flexes, so a fixed price per time box matches how the work is managed.

whyNot.0: The final product's scope is not known up front, so a single fixed price is hard to set fairly.
whyNot.1: Lines of code are not a meaningful unit of value and would reward the wrong behaviour.
whyNot.2: Cost plus fee can work, but never without cost control, because the buyer carries the cost risk.

reteach.title: Getting your car repaired
reteach.question: A garage could charge you for car repairs in four different ways. Which way protects you best, and when?

blocks.h: Four ways to pay the garage
blocks.body: 'A new clutch is £400, fitted' is fixed price: if it takes longer, that's the garage's problem, but adding a service costs extra. 'We'll strip it down and charge parts and labour at cost, plus 15%' is cost plus fee: fair when nobody knows what's wrong, but you carry the risk. '£80 per tyre' is per unit quantity: you pay for however many need replacing. 'We think £600; if it's less we split the saving, if more we split the extra' is target cost.

blocks.text: You would only accept 'parts and labour plus 15%' if nobody yet knows what is wrong, and you would want to see the receipts. That is exactly why cost plus fee needs strong cost control.

explain.body: A lump sum agreed up front for a defined scope. The supplier carries the cost risk, so it needs a well-defined, stable scope. Changes are priced as variations and can be costly.

explain.h: Is fixed price a good fit?

test.q: Which condition is MOST needed for a fixed price contract to work well?
options: A well-defined, stable scope
A scope expected to change a lot
No idea of the quantities needed
Open-book access to all costs
test.why: A supplier can only commit to a lump sum when it knows exactly what it is delivering, so the scope must be well defined and stable.

whyNot.1: Frequent change makes fixed price costly, because every change becomes a variation.
whyNot.2: Uncertain quantities suit per unit quantity.
whyNot.3: Open-book cost access is typical of cost plus and target cost arrangements.

explain.body: The buyer reimburses actual costs plus a fixed or percentage fee. The buyer carries the cost risk. It suits uncertain scope but needs strong cost control, because the supplier has little incentive to save.

test.q: Under a cost plus fee contract, what does the buyer need MOST to protect itself?
options: A frozen, detailed specification
A guaranteed number of units
Strong control and audit of costs
A pain/gain share with the supplier
test.why: The buyer pays actual costs, so it needs strong cost control: open-book records, audits and approval of spend.

whyNot.0: Cost plus is chosen precisely because the scope cannot be frozen.
whyNot.1: Units relate to per unit quantity contracts.
whyNot.3: A pain/gain share is the defining feature of target cost.

explain.body: An agreed rate is paid for each unit delivered (per metre, tonne, item). Also called a schedule of rates or remeasurement. It suits repeated, measurable work where the quantity is uncertain.

items.label: fixed per unit: the supplier's risk
measured as delivered: the buyer's risk

test.q: Why is a per unit quantity (schedule of rates) contract chosen for repeated work such as laying kerbs?
options: The total price is fixed before work starts
Quantities are uncertain but units measurable
The supplier carries all the quantity risk
No measuring of completed work is needed
test.why: Per unit quantity suits repeated, measurable work where nobody knows exactly how many units will be needed.

whyNot.0: Only the rate is fixed; the total depends on how many units are delivered.
whyNot.2: The buyer carries the quantity risk; the supplier carries the rate.
whyNot.3: Completed units must be measured to calculate payment.

explain.body: An agreed target, with overruns (pain) and savings (gain) shared between buyer and supplier by an agreed mechanism. It incentivises collaboration and efficiency.

test.q: What is the main purpose of the pain/gain mechanism in a target cost contract?
options: To let the buyer avoid paying any overrun
To fix the final price before work begins
To pay the supplier for each unit delivered
To give both sides a stake in beating target
test.why: Sharing overruns and savings gives both parties a financial reason to work together efficiently and beat the target.

whyNot.0: Overruns are shared, so the buyer pays its share.
whyNot.1: Fixing the final price up front is fixed price.
whyNot.2: Paying per unit delivered is per unit quantity.
